content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper conducts an overall evaluation of the backdoor threats in the supply chain of one representative self-supervised model - Masked Image Modelling. It evaluates the influence factors of the attack effectiveness in each step of the supply chain: pre-train phase, release phase, and downstream task phase.  It also evaluates the effectiveness of existing defenses against the attacks in these phases.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
+ This paper well states the background and gives a comprehensive summarization of the existing works. 
+ The experiments are well-designed. The paper conducted a large-scale evaluation of different datasets to come up with the corresponding findings. 

Weaknesses: 
- My first concern about the paper is Section 3. I could understand the Type I attack, where the attack goal is very clear, i.e., fool the downstream classification task. Regarding type II and type III, they are not clearly stated or justified. First, about the attack goal and threat model. In these two cases, the attacker should have zero knowledge about the downstream task. It is not that clear how to generate the attack under this strong constraint. If an attacker implants backdoors based on classification task A, say a binary classification task on datasets. What if the infected model is actually used for task B: a mutil-class classification on the same or a different dataset? This is possible and practical. Will the attack still be effective in this case? The paper does not clearly state the threat model for attack types II and III, which may cause some confusion. Regarding the attack techniques, type II uses an existing attack. The paper claims it proposes a new attack for type III. Across the paper, I didn't find a description of this proposed attack technique. Section 3 only mentions it increases the trigger number to 9, without providing the whole workflow. Like how to inject triggers; what is the training objective function; what is the difference between the proposed method and Saha et al. 2021? Since this part is the main technical contribution of this work, I would suggest the authors make it more clear. 

- Although the experiment is comprehensive and large-scale, the significance of the findings is not well justified. Section 5 reveals the key influence factors of each attack type. What would be the utilities of these findings? As an attacker, it could guide me to launch strong attacks without exhaustively searching for good hyper-parameters, or providing some guidance about how to tune the parameters. What about the defense side? How do the findings guide defense development? I would highly suggest the authors provide some discussion along this direction and state the meaning and utilities of the findings in this paper. It helps improve the value and impact of this work. Otherwise, they are more like "good to know" stuff. 

- This is similar to Section 6, the evaluation of defense. It is not surprising that existing defenses fall short for certain types of attacks. How we can leverage the findings to build stronger defenses is more interesting and important. Besides, the authors do not include one type of defenses that trains robust models from poisoned datasets (e.g., [Rab: provable robustness against backdoor attacks]).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: As discussed above, certain parts of the attacks considered in this work are not that clear, which affects the paper's clarity and reproducibility. But, this is not that hard to address. With additional details, the results should be reproducible. The novelty of the paper is limited because 1. this work mostly uses existing techniques; 2. The findings are not that exciting and significant. Since the experimental design is relatively comprehensive. I would rank the overall quality as fair.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper conducts a relatively comprehensive evaluation of the backdoor threats in the supply chain of MIM. As specified above, the technical contribution is relatively thin, and the significances of the findings are not well justified. As such, I believe this paper may below the bar of ICLR.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.

content.details_of_ethics_concerns: Since this paper studies the security of DNN models, it would be great to include an ethical statement. For example, attackers may leverage the results of this work to launch strong attacks, etc.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the backdoor threat against masked image modeling in different phases. The adversary could plant backdoor triggers in pretraining, model release, and downstream tasks. Particularly, the pretraining phase is the most difficult, while the downstream tasks are comparably easier. This paper identifies the number of triggers in the image, and the trigger pattern is the key to successfully planting a backdoor in the pretraining phase. Several defenses have been investigated, but no successful method can detect attacks in the model release phase.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
---
Strength  
- Thoroughly investigated the backdoor threat in different phases and proposed a backdoor attack method that can successfully plant the trigger in the pre-training phase. All existing methods fail to achieve this. 
- Empirical experiments focused exploration of backdoor vulnerability in MIM, which covered most of the contributing factors of backdoor attacks. 
- Attack taxonomy could be applied to all different self-supervised training settings. 

---
Weaknesses
- Section 3, "i.e., pre-training, release, and downstream phases." and "We name the backdoor attacks in each phase as Type I, Type II, and Type III attacks, respectively..." However, Type I is for downstream phases, and III is for the pre-training phase. I suggest altering the ordering in this statement. 
- The defense methods studied in this work are all based on the data poisoning threat model. It is not surprising that it has limited effectiveness against Type II attacks. It would be interesting to look into other backdoor model detection methods. See [1,2,3] as examples. 
- Limited contribution in terms of attack methods. Type I/II are all based on existing works. Type I and II attacks can successfully attack MIM models are not surprising. Type III attacks are interesting. One existing method (Saha et al., 2021) has investigated contrastive learning rather than MIM. However, the proposed Type III-M is trivial that placing the trigger in different regions to avoid masking.
- "To address this issue, the attacker in Type III attack only poisons samples..." This sentence is too long and hard to follow.
- Descriptions of the Type III threat model are not clear. Does the adversary need to have access to both pre-training and downstream data? Or only pre-training data? There should not have label information in pre-training phase. This part needs further clarification.
- There are also label-consistency issues. Pre-training and downstream dataset could have different labelling policies. For one, CIFAR-10 has one class of dog, while ImageNet has different breeds. This could affect the results of Type III attacks. It's unclear how the targeted class is selected in the experiments and whether the labeling difference could affect the proposed method. 

[1] Detecting ai trojans using meta neural analysis. S&P 2021. \
[2] AEVA: Black-box Backdoor Detection Using Adversarial Extreme Value Analysis. ICLR 2022. \
[3] Practical detection of trojan neural networks: Data-limited and data-free cases. ECCV 2020.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper explores the robustness and vulnerability of the recently proposed masked image modeling (MIM) methods (MAE and CAE taken as the main examples) under the risk of backdoor attacks. The authors provide a systematic study by digging into the pre-training, release and downstream phases separately, with clear explanations about the goals, taxonomy and capabilities. Finally, an empirical study about the detection performance is further provided, strongly motivating future researches on backdoor attacks of MIM models.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
- Strength:
  - This is overall a quite well-prepared paper with abundant discussions about both the backdoor attacks and detections supported by extensive experimental results.
  - The authors provide a detailed introduction about the goals, taxonomy and capability of the adversary, which is important for readers unfamiliar with this topic.
  - Extensive experiment details are provided in the Appendix.
- Weakness:
  - Novelty:
    - Novelty, especially technical novelty, would be a controversial problem about this paper.
    - Although this paper, as the authors claim, is the first work to discuss the robustness and vulnerability of MIM under backdoor attacks, the attack methods, the trigger patterns and the detection methods are all proposed by previous works. The only technical novelty of this paper is to use more triggers to deal with the large mask ratio of MAE in Tab. 5.
  - Experiments:
    - Experiments in Sec. 4.2 show that the downstream phase might be the most vulnerable, which is actually understandable, since the transfer process is a full-supervised process regardless of the pre-training method. I wonder if there are any differences between supervised, contrastive [1] and MIM pre-training for Type 1 Attack?
    - In Sec. 5, the authors claim that the success factor of Type 3 Attack is the number of triggers. I wonder if this is also connected with the large mask ratio used in MAE. It would be interesting to see an ablation about the relationship between trigger number and mask ratio.
  - Clarification:
    - For Type3 attack, the attacker needs to put triggers on images of target classes. But how to do that considering the pre-training dataset is totally unlabeled, or is it just an assumed setting given the pre-training dataset is ImageNet?
    - In Sec. 6, the 4th line should be "We evaluate the performance of backdoor attack detections" instead of "We evaluate the performance of backdoor attacks".

[1] Jinyuan Jia, Yupei Liu, and Neil Zhenqiang Gong. BadEncoder: Backdoor Attacks to Pre-trained Encoders in Self-Supervised Learning. In IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P). IEEE, 2022.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies how to successfully inject backdoor attacks in ViTs pretrained by MIM methods. The findings and novelty seems limited to me. Please see comments below.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Some key findings in this paper include:

1. If using a square trigger, the trigger should occur multiple times in the single image, in order for the attack to succeed. 

This seems trivial finding to me, since the MIM masks input image at a very high masking rate and thus a single local square trigger is likely to be masked out and voided for injecting backdoors. A trivial solution, as proposed by the authors, is to largely increase the poisoning ratio in the training set and repeat the local trigger in a single image. Although these methods can increase attack success rate (ASR), they also make the attack harder (in practice it is not easy for the attacker to inject a large portion of poisoned images to the training set) and more noticible. Also, these solutions are also some first-to-try solutions when general attacks does not success. Overall, they are trivial solution and has serious limitations. 

One more interesting thing to do is to check whether global backdoor patterns, such as in Blend attack, Smooth attack, trojan water mark, etc., which adds trigger on the entire image, work for MIM. 


2. White trigger doens't work well on MIM compared with colored triggers. 

This is also trivial to me. Stronger pattern leads to better ASR, as everyone would expect. The more interesting thing to do is how to generate the "optimal" trigger for MIM. It can be either global or local. Will it depend on the visual word size? Will it depend on the distribution of the training set? These are all open questions which matter but failed to be reported in the paper.
content.correctness: 1: The main claims of the paper are incorrect or not at all supported by theory or empirical results.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.
